strengths: The paper targets a genuine limitation of MLP-Mixer architectures (lack of causality) and proposes a simple, well-specified remedy: an upper-triangular masked weight (Eqs. 11-13) that provably restricts each output time step to depend only on past inputs. The mechanism is clearly described and easy to verify.

The cluster-aware multi-embedding idea is sensible and well-motivated: grouping channels via spectral clustering on correlation profiles and giving each cluster a dedicated embedding layer avoids imposing artificial dependencies across unrelated channels. The parameter-count analysis (Section 3.2.2) and the spurious-correlation analysis in Appendix G (Algorithm 2, Table 8) provide mechanistic evidence beyond just F1 gains.

The sequential anomaly-scoring scheme (Eqs. 14-17), which accumulates log-p-value evidence against validation-set reconstruction losses and includes a reset condition and span delineation, is a reasonable online alternative to offline robust normalization used in SensitiveHUE, and Table 3 shows consistent improvements over point-based thresholding.

Evaluation covers six standard benchmarks with 15 baselines, reports means/standard deviations over three seeds (Table 7), GFLOPs, hyperparameter search ranges (Table 6), detailed preprocessing (Appendix C), and an honest Limitations appendix (Appendix H), including the sensitivity to alpha and the residual spurious-correlation issue. The authors fairly separate SensitiveHUE (Offline) vs. (Online) and refrain from point-adjust inflation.
Ablations address the right questions: with/without clustering, causal vs. non-causal vs. no temporal mixer, and three alternative clustering variants (Table 5), with M optimized per variant.
weaknesses: The reported comparison in Table 2 largely copies baseline numbers from the NPSR and SensitiveHUE papers rather than re-running them under a unified protocol. Given that preprocessing, downsampling, thresholding, and evaluation protocols differ across those papers, the headline improvement percentages (e.g., 10-12%) are difficult to interpret as apples-to-apples. Only SensitiveHUE was re-run by the authors.

The central evaluation protocol uses 'best F1', with alpha (Eq. 14) and threshold h explicitly searched 'to get the best F1 score' (Appendix D). This is oracle threshold selection on test data, which inflates scores and, more importantly for this paper, undermines the claimed suitability for 'online/real-time' detection: in practice neither h nor alpha would be tuned on the test stream. No sensitivity analysis of F1 vs. h or alpha is provided to show robustness of the operating point.

The ablation study (Tables 4 and 5) is restricted to only two datasets (SWaT and PSM). Several of the claimed conclusions rest on small margins: e.g., full model 0.883 vs. 0.875 (Case 9) on SWaT, a gap of the same order as the reported standard deviations for multi-entity datasets, so the evidence that the causal mixer (rather than the clustering) drives gains is not established beyond SWaT/PSM, and no significance testing is reported.

The causal-vs-non-causal claim is only partially supported by the data: Case-8 (non-causal, clustered) vs. Case-10 (causal, clustered) helps on PSM (0.652 vs. 0.716) and modestly on SWaT (0.871 vs. 0.883), but elsewhere in the table the non-causal configurations are not consistently worse (e.g., Case-2, non-causal without clustering, beats several clustered variants on SWaT). The narrative overstates what the table shows.

The backward-search span extension (Eqs. 16-17) is applied after a detection segment ends and uses beta values over the whole flagged region, i.e., future information relative to the alarm time; the 'online' framing is thus not fully accurate for the reported segment-level F1.

Novelty is moderate: causal masking of linear layers is a direct analog of attention masking, spectral clustering on correlations is standard, and the evidence-accumulation scoring closely resembles existing sequential/CUSUM-style and p-value thresholding approaches (e.g., SPOT-like methods), which are not discussed. The related work does not engage with sequential-change-detection literature from which Eq. 15 is essentially derived.

No code release is mentioned despite detailed hyperparameter listings; reproducibility of the full pipeline (Optuna searches per dataset, per-entity training, preprocessing choices copied from prior work) would be hard without it.

Minor presentation issues: the Table 4 caption defines the x/check symbols as 'presence and absence', which is the reverse of the usage described in Section 4.2.2; Eq. 10's floor/rounding can produce inconsistent dimension allocations for skewed cluster sizes; typos and inconsistent notation (e.g., Theta_u vs. Theta_n, L2 underlined inconsistently) appear throughout the method section.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the proposed architecture (cluster-aware multi-embedding plus a causally masked MLP-Mixer) is described with sufficient mathematical detail, including pseudocode for the spectral clustering procedure (Algorithm 1) and the anomaly scoring accumulation rule (Eqs. 14-17).

Results are reported without point-adjustment F1, which is the more rigorous evaluation protocol, and the authors explicitly justify this choice and distinguish online vs. offline variants of the strongest baseline (SensitiveHUE).

The paper includes several useful ablations: a 10-configuration modular ablation (Table 4), comparisons against three alternative channel-clustering schemes with tuned M (Table 5), a point-based vs. sequential scoring comparison (Table 3), a spurious-correlation analysis (Appendix G, Algorithm 2), and seed-robustness plus GFLOPs reporting (Table 7).

The limitations appendix is candid, acknowledging sensitivity to α, the expansion-factor/causality constraint in the temporal mixer, and the fact that clustering does not fully remove spurious correlations.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol undermines the paper's central 'online/real-time' claim. The reported F1 is the 'best F1', obtained by tuning the threshold h, the significance parameter α, the number of clusters M, and other hyperparameters per dataset to maximize F1 on the test set (Sections 4.2, Appendix D). This contradicts the criticism the authors direct at SensitiveHUE's offline normalization, which also requires test-set access. A truly online evaluation with validation-set threshold selection, or rolling evaluation, is needed to support the online claim.

The baseline comparison is not reproducible or like-for-like: most baseline F1 scores are copied from the NPSR and SensitiveHUE papers rather than re-run under the authors' preprocessing (which includes dataset-specific steps such as zeroing channels, moving-average filtering, and downsampling; Appendix C). Differences in preprocessing alone can move F1 substantially on these benchmarks, so the claimed improvements (e.g., 10-12% on PSM/MSL/SMD) may not be attributable to the method.

No confidence intervals or seed variance are reported for the comparison in Table 2; variance is only reported for the proposed model in Appendix E. Some improvements (e.g., 0.524 vs. 0.524 on SMAP, 0.883 vs. 0.874 on SWaT vs. online SensitiveHUE) are within plausible seed noise.

Novelty is limited and overstated. Masking a linear/MLP layer to enforce causality is a standard technique, per-cluster or per-channel embedding of multivariate time series is well explored, and evidence-accumulation scoring with p-values against a validation loss distribution closely resembles existing sequential scoring / extreme-value thresholding approaches (e.g., SPOT-style methods and NPSR's sequential reconstruction). The claim of being 'the first work to introduce causality into the MLP-Mixer architecture' is a narrow technical distinction rather than a conceptual advance.

The ablation studies are conducted on only two of six datasets (SWAT and PSM), and gains from individual modules are small in isolation (e.g., Case-9 → Case-10: 0.875 → 0.883 on SWAT; 0.681 → 0.716 on PSM), so the attribution of the headline improvements to specific components is weakly supported. The full-model advantage over the best non-full configurations is not always consistent across the two datasets.

Key design choices are under-justified: the number of clusters M is selected via Silhouette score plus Optuna test-F1 optimization, so Table 5's comparison across variants with 'optimized M' partially reflects test-set tuning rather than intrinsic clustering quality; the choice of cosine similarity between correlation profiles as the graph affinity is not theoretically motivated.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and the method has a large hyperparameter surface (M, d, df, L, δ, α, h, learning rate) searched with Optuna, making exact reproduction of the reported numbers difficult from the manuscript alone.

Significance is moderate: the contribution is an incremental combination of known components applied to a benchmark-heavy subfield where evaluation practice is already contested; the paper does not provide analysis (e.g., on real streaming data, latency, or drift) demonstrating practical online deployment value beyond benchmark F1.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper targets genuinely online multivariate time-series anomaly detection and explicitly avoids point-adjusted F1, which is a known inflated metric — this is more rigorous evaluation practice than much of the competing literature.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: six public benchmarks, 15 baselines, results obtained (for some baselines) by running the authors' public code rather than only copying numbers, and a fair online/offline distinction for SensitiveHUE.

Reasonably thorough ablations: modular architecture ablations (Table 4), clustering-variant comparisons (Table 5, Appendix F), a spurious-correlation analysis (Appendix G), repeated runs with standard deviations (Table 7), and a detailed hyperparameter search description (Appendix D).

Honest limitations discussion (Appendix H): the authors candidly identify sensitivity to α, the expansion-factor causality caveat, and the fact that spurious correlations are reduced but not eliminated by clustering.
Reproducibility is aided by complete hyperparameter ranges, preprocessing details, hardware/software specifications, and pseudocode for the clustering and spurious-correlation procedures.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The causal temporal mixer is essentially a masked linear layer (a standard technique, cf. MADE-style masking or causal convolutions), and spectral clustering of channels plus per-cluster embeddings is a straightforward combination of known components. The claim of being the 'first work to introduce causality into MLP-Mixer' is plausible but a modest contribution for a main-track paper.

The central evaluation metric ('best F1', with threshold h and α searched per dataset via Optuna) constitutes oracle threshold tuning on the test set. This practice is common in the field but directly tensions with the paper's central claim of suitability for online, real-time detection; the method's hyperparameters (α, h, δ) are dataset-tuned while baseline tuning is inherited from prior papers, making cross-model comparisons uneven.

Evidence for the key ablation claims is thin and modest in magnitude: the causal-vs-non-causal comparison (Case 9 vs 10) differs by 0.008 (SWAT) and 0.035 (PSM), and the 10-case ablation is run on only two datasets; no statistical significance testing is reported for these or the Table 5 clustering-variant differences.
A numerical inconsistency: Table 7 reports a mean F1 of 0.564 (std 0.025) for SMAP, which exceeds the best reported F1 of 0.524 in Table 2 — this is internally inconsistent and needs explanation.

Many baseline numbers are transcribed from the NPSR and SensitiveHUE papers rather than re-run under identical preprocessing, introducing protocol-mismatch risk; no baseline FLOPs/latency comparison is provided, so the efficiency claims for the cluster-aware embedding are not contextualized.

The sequential anomaly detection method (p-value-based evidence accumulation with reset logic) has several hand-designed components (Eq. 14–17) whose design choices are not ablated (e.g., δ, the reset rule), and its relation to prior sequential scoring methods (e.g., NPSR) could be more clearly differentiated.
No explicit code release is stated, which limits reproducibility given the many dataset-specific preprocessing steps.

strengths: The paper is well motivated: it identifies a genuine gap (MLP-Mixer models for time series lack temporal causality) and addresses it with a simple, principled causal weight mask (Eq. 11-13) analogous to causal attention masking, with a 1/j normalization justified by optimization stability.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: six benchmark datasets, 23 baselines spanning many method families, three evaluation protocols for multi-entity datasets, PR AUC, VUS PR/ROC, R-F1/Aff-F1, an ADD-FAP trade-off analysis for the online setting, computational cost comparisons, and robustness results over five random seeds with error bars.

The ablations directly support the core claims: the causal vs. non-causal temporal mixer comparison (Table 5, Cases 6/8 vs. 10), a gradient-based verification that the causal mixer eliminates future-input influence (Figure 3), clustering variant comparisons (Table 7), and NN-separability and spurious-correlation analyses (Tables 6, 14) that probe why clustering helps.

The sequential anomaly scoring method receives a proper statistical treatment: Appendix A derives the distribution of the evidence term beta_t under the null and a condition (alpha < e^-1) under which the expected evidence is negative, giving the accumulation scheme (a CUSUM-like procedure) a principled footing.

The online applicability of the scoring method is clearly argued and contrasted with SensitiveHUE's offline robust normalization, and the offline/online distinction is carefully handled when comparing against that baseline.
The paper is generally well written, with an honest limitations section (Appendix M) that correctly scopes the 'causality' claim to temporal causality rather than inter-channel causal discovery.
weaknesses: The primary metric (best-F1) is obtained by sweeping both the threshold h and the significance parameter alpha to maximize F1 on the test labels (Eq. 24, Appendix F), and hyperparameters (including the number of clusters M, via Optuna with F1 feedback) appear to be selected against test performance. This inflates absolute scores and makes comparisons against baselines whose numbers are transcribed from other papers (Table 8) somewhat fragile; PR AUC partially mitigates but does not remove this concern.

The architectural novelty is modest. The causal mixer is a standard upper-triangular weight mask on MLP-Mixer temporal mixing (cf. WaveNet/transformer masking), and the sequential scoring is essentially a CUSUM-style p-value accumulator; the contributions are more a well-engineered combination than a fundamentally new method, and the paper does not engage with the CUSUM/sequential-change-point literature it is closest to.

Some ablation effects are small relative to reported seed variability. In Table 5, the causal vs. non-causal gap on SWAT is 0.883 vs. 0.871, while Table 12 reports seed standard deviations up to ~0.03 for F1; the claim that non-causal mixing 'does not effectively capture temporal information' is stronger than this evidence strictly supports, particularly under the optimistic best-F1 protocol.

The claimed benefits of cluster-aware embedding are inconsistent across datasets: the NN-sep improvement is 39% on SWAT but only 3.8% on WADI and 0.06% on PSM (Table 6), and a few channels show increased spurious correlation after clustering (negative delta in Table 14), which weakens the generality of the spurious-correlation mitigation narrative.

Baseline scores are collected from heterogeneous sources (original papers and later works) under possibly different preprocessing, window sizes, and protocols; only a few baselines (TimesNet, xLSTMAD, SensitiveHUE-Online) were re-run. The paper acknowledges this, but cross-source comparability remains a concern for the headline improvements.

Minor presentation issues: the code URL in the Figure 1 caption is left empty ('Code is available at:'), the main-text results report single best-F1 numbers without confidence intervals (error bars are relegated to Appendix I), and Table 3 omits the strong offline SensitiveHUE variant that appears in Table 2.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 23 baselines across six standard benchmarks, three evaluation protocols for multi-entity datasets, and multiple metrics (best-F1, PR AUC, VUS-PR/ROC), which exceeds the typical rigor in this subfield.

The treatment of online vs. offline baselines is fair and thoughtful: the authors explicitly flag that SensitiveHUE's robust normalization uses the entire test set and construct an 'Online' variant for comparison, plus an ADD-FAP trade-off analysis (Fig. 8), which is appropriate for an online detection claim.
Verification that the causal mixer truly eliminates future information leakage via input-gradient analysis (Fig. 3) is a nice, concrete check beyond simply asserting the mask works.

Extensive ablations (Tables 4-7, Appendix J), robustness over five seeds (Table 12), computational cost comparison (Table 13), and an honest limitations section (Appendix M) that correctly scopes 'causality' to temporal causality only.
weaknesses: Limited originality: each component is a straightforward recombination of known ideas — upper-triangular weight masking on a linear layer is the standard autoregressive/Transformer masking trick applied to an MLP-Mixer; per-group embeddings from clustering is a common channel-grouping heuristic; and the sequential scoring (Eq. 14-17) is essentially a CUSUM-style running sum of empirical p-values, a well-worn change-detection device. No component is technically deep or surprising.

The headline claim (causal mixing improves detection) is not well supported by the paper's own evidence: Table 5 shows the causal vs. non-causal temporal mixer differs by ~0.008-0.012 F1 on SWAT and PSM, comparable to the no-mixer condition; Table 4 shows point-based MSE thresholding already achieves 0.882 on SWAT vs. 0.883 for the full pipeline. Much of the gain on MSL/SMD/WADI comes from the sequential scoring method rather than the architecture, and Table 4 has no variance reported, so these small margins may not be meaningful.

Evaluation protocol inflates results: Best-F1 is defined (Eq. 24) as the max over a two-dimensional sweep of both α and h on the test set, and hyperparameters are 'tuned for each experiment separately' including for every ablation case. Sweeping two hyperparameters on test labels is an oracle protocol that systematically favors the proposed method and makes the small ablation deltas unreliable, even if threshold sweeping is common in this literature.

Reproducibility is undermined: the code availability statement in Figure 1 ('Code is available at:') is followed by an empty link, so despite the detailed appendix, others cannot currently verify or build on the work. Some baseline numbers are also copied from other papers' reports under possibly different preprocessing, which the authors acknowledge but do not fully resolve.

The statistical grounding of the scoring method is heuristic: the uniformity of the empirical p-values under normal data is assumed despite the authors themselves noting temporal dependence in the reconstruction losses (Appendix A), so the 'statistically grounded' framing of the evidence accumulation is weaker than presented.

Mixed headline results: on PR AUC (Table 3) the model is not best on PSM, and improvements are uneven (e.g., modest on SMAP under some protocols); the abstract's 'consistently achieves superior performance' overstates the evidence.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the proposed framework (causal temporal mixer + cluster-aware multi-embedding + sequential anomaly scoring) is coherently motivated; the distinction between temporal causality and Granger/inter-channel causality is explicitly and honestly drawn (Appendix M).

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: six benchmarks, 23 baselines, three evaluation protocols for multi-entity datasets, PR-AUC/VUS metrics, ADD-FAP trade-off analysis, 5-seed robustness comparison (Table 12), computational cost comparison (Table 13), and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (Appendix J.3).

The gradient-based verification of causality (Section 4.2.5, Figure 3) is a convincing empirical check that the masked mixer eliminates future information leakage, directly supporting a central claim.

The sequential scoring method receives a genuine statistical treatment: the p-value/evidence formulation, the boundary-correction equations, and the statistical interpretation in Appendix A (including the derivation showing E0[β] < 0 for α < e^{-1}) give the scoring mechanism a principled grounding rather than being a purely heuristic smoothing.

The ablation study (Table 5, 7, 14) isolates each component, compares clustering variants, and includes the NN-sep separability and spurious-correlation analyses, which is more evidence than typical TSAD papers provide.
The online/offline distinction for SensitiveHUE is handled fairly, with the authors reproducing the online variant rather than only quoting the stronger offline numbers.
weaknesses: The primary metric, best-F1, is obtained by sweeping both α and h directly on the test set (Eq. 24, Appendix F). This is an oracle-tuned result and inflates all numbers; combined with per-dataset Optuna tuning, the reported margins may not reflect deployable performance. While the practice is common in this literature, the paper's central 'consistently superior performance' claim rests on it, and no validation-based threshold selection is evaluated.

Baseline comparability is weakened: many baseline numbers are copied from other papers under different preprocessing, tuning budgets, and evaluation protocols (Table 8, e.g., D3R from SimAD, DAGMM from NPSR), while the proposed method receives its own per-dataset tuning. Only three baselines are reproduced by the authors.

The contribution of the causal mixer itself is technically modest — it is a masked linear layer (equivalent to causal convolutions/MADE-style masking) with a 1/j scaling — and the paper's own ablations show gains are mixed: point-based detection on SWAT achieves F1 0.882 vs. 0.883 with the full sequential method (Table 4), non-causal Case-8 is not dominated by the causal variant on PSM in all configurations, and clustering improves NN-sep by only 0.06% on PSM (Table 6).

There are internal inconsistencies between headline and robustness results: Table 2 reports SMD F1 of 0.612/0.602 while the 5-seed Table 12 reports 0.507 ± 0.068, and PSM 0.716 vs. 0.688 ± 0.022, suggesting the headline numbers may reflect favorable seeds or protocol-2 vs protocol-3 confusion that is not fully clarified.

Some evidence for the cluster-aware embedding is weak or partially contradictory: spurious-correlation reduction is negative for several PSM channels (Table 14, e.g., −49.2%, −12.9%), and the improvement narrative is strongest only for SWAT.

The code link in Figure 1 is empty ('Code is available at:'), and despite detailed hyperparameter tables, no artifact is provided, hurting reproducibility of the full pipeline (spectral clustering setup, Optuna configurations, seeds).

The statistical approximation in Appendix A assumes p-values are approximately uniform despite acknowledged temporal correlation in reconstruction losses; the resulting negative-drift guarantee is heuristic, and the large accumulated score magnitudes (e.g., s_t ≈ 3500 in Figure 5) suggest the ε-regularization makes the theory only loosely connected to practice.
